# Version { #crossrepo.Version }

```python
crossrepo.Version(
    sha,
    date,
    subject,
    blob,
    size,
    lfs_oid=None,
    parts=0,
    tags=(),
    link=None,
    missing=False,
)
```

One commit in which a result file changed.

A version is defined by a commit, not by a repository tag. Analysis repos
are rarely tagged, whereas every change to a result file is a commit, so
commits give a version key that exists without extra discipline. Tags, when
present, are carried in `tags` and can be used to address a version, but
they never define one.

## Attributes {.doc-section .doc-section-attributes}

<code>[**sha**]{.parameter-name} [:]{.parameter-annotation-sep} [[str](`str`)]{.parameter-annotation}</code>

:   Full sha of the commit the repository pointed at. This is the user-facing version key, written out in full so that it also means something to git and to GitHub without crossrepo in hand.

<code>[**date**]{.parameter-name} [:]{.parameter-annotation-sep} [[str](`str`)]{.parameter-annotation}</code>

:   Committer date in ISO-8601 format.

<code>[**subject**]{.parameter-name} [:]{.parameter-annotation-sep} [[str](`str`)]{.parameter-annotation}</code>

:   Subject line of the commit.

<code>[**blob**]{.parameter-name} [:]{.parameter-annotation-sep} [[str](`str`)]{.parameter-annotation}</code>

:   Content key of the file at this commit, and the key it is cached under. Ordinarily the git blob sha, which is a hash of the content. For a dataset held in a directory it is the git tree sha, which hashes the whole directory and so plays the same part; for a file published as a link it is the ``sha256`` its manifest stamp records, git holding only the link and not the bytes behind it.

<code>[**size**]{.parameter-name} [:]{.parameter-annotation-sep} [[int](`int`)]{.parameter-annotation}</code>

:   Size in bytes, resolved through Git LFS pointers so that it is the size of the real content rather than of the pointer. For a dataset it is the total over its files.

<code>[**lfs_oid**]{.parameter-name} [:]{.parameter-annotation-sep} [[Optional](`typing.Optional`)\[[str](`str`)\]]{.parameter-annotation}</code>

:   The sha256 object id when the file is stored in Git LFS, else `None`.

<code>[**parts**]{.parameter-name} [:]{.parameter-annotation-sep} [[int](`int`)]{.parameter-annotation}</code>

:   Number of files the version is made of. Zero for an ordinary file; for a dataset published as a directory, the count of files beneath it.

<code>[**tags**]{.parameter-name} [:]{.parameter-annotation-sep} [[Tuple](`typing.Tuple`)\[[str](`str`), ...\]]{.parameter-annotation}</code>

:   Any tags pointing at this commit.

<code>[**link**]{.parameter-name} [:]{.parameter-annotation-sep} [[Optional](`typing.Optional`)\[[str](`str`)\]]{.parameter-annotation}</code>

:   Target of the symbolic link the file is published as, as committed, or `None` for a file git holds the content of. A link's content is read from the target rather than from git, and `blob` is then the stamp that says which content it should be.

<code>[**missing**]{.parameter-name} [:]{.parameter-annotation-sep} [[bool](`bool`)]{.parameter-annotation}</code>

:   Whether the content is not where it should be: that a `link` resolved to nothing when the catalog was built. Always `False` for content git holds itself, which is there wherever the repository is. It is recorded rather than worked out on demand because the answer is a question for the machine the repository is on, and asking it over ssh costs a round trip; it is therefore as old as the catalog, and a pipeline that writes the file after the last scan still reads as missing until the next one.  It says the repository cannot produce the content, which is the question a listing is asking. The cache is a separate matter: content already in it -- fetched before the file went away, or put there by another file of the same bytes -- is still handed over, since a cached object is what it is whatever became of the link.
